attacks.claim: The plan makes hosted, closed-source Cirrus Cloud the sole sync backend in 5.0 and archives the stride-server image, breaking the published promise that users can self-host sync and own their workout data. No post-5.0 self-hosting path is defined.
attacks.evidence: "after which Cirrus Cloud becomes the single sync backend and the stride-server Docker image is archived" / "the server component is available only as the hosted Cirrus Cloud service"

attacks.claim: All workouts and GPS tracks are replicated to a third-party commercial cloud with no stated consent, opt-out, local-only option, data-processing terms, data location, or encryption. Existing self-hosted users are moved to a vendor they did not choose.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: consent, opt-out, DPA, data residency, encryption; "Cirrus replicates to Cirrus Cloud when connectivity returns"

attacks.claim: The core durability promise (record-level resumable uploads so a dropped connection never leaves a partial workout) rests on an unverified vendor claim. The spike that would verify it is scheduled for Week 1, after the plan is already dispatched to three contributors.
attacks.evidence: "uploads are resumable at the record level, so a dropped connection never leaves a partial workout" / "Week 1: Cirrus integration spike"

attacks.claim: Migration has no integrity check on the backup before the source is migrated, no idempotency or checkpoint reconciliation for chunked writes, and no defined behavior for downgrade after backup deletion. A failed or partial migration can silently lose data or duplicate workouts, the exact failure class the plan targets.
attacks.evidence: "the app copies the existing SQLite database to stride-backup-v3.db before migrating into the Cirrus store" / "resumable if the app is killed mid-migration"

attacks.claim: There is no export or exit path from the Cirrus store or Cloud back to a vendor-neutral or self-hostable format, and the SDK is closed binary. If Cirrus changes pricing or shuts down, the project has no reversible way to restore sync for ~90k users.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: export/migration path from Cirrus; "distributed as a prebuilt binary ... under the Cirrus commercial license"

attacks.claim: A proprietary, commercially licensed binary SDK and hosted-only server are being introduced as the sole sync path into an MIT-licensed open-source app, with no license-compatibility review or contract. Licensing constraints and the commitment to users are not evaluated before crossing the gate.
attacks.evidence: "distributed as a prebuilt binary (iOS xcframework, Android AAR) under the Cirrus commercial license"

attacks.claim: Tombstones expire after 90 days, so an offline device returning later can resurrect deleted workouts, contradicting the stated goal. Clock skew on device-stamped HLC values is also unaddressed, so a future-stamped edit can permanently win.
attacks.evidence: "Deletes are tombstones retained 90 days so an offline device cannot resurrect a deleted workout." / "per-field last-writer-wins using a hybrid logical clock stamped on device"

attacks.claim: Client authentication to Cirrus Cloud, credential storage on device, server-side per-user isolation, and server validation of client-stamped HLC values and tombstones are not specified. A forged tombstone or timestamp could hide or overwrite another user's records.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: auth, credential storage, server ownership checks; "a hybrid logical clock stamped on device"

attacks.claim: The migration writes an unencrypted plaintext copy of the full SQLite database (including GPS) and keeps it 30+ days, with no encryption, file-permission, or backup-exclusion requirement. The 3.x restore also has no integrity check, so a tampered backup could inject data that then syncs to the server.
attacks.evidence: "copies the existing SQLite database to stride-backup-v3.db" / "3.x detects stride-backup-v3.db and restores from it"

attacks.claim: Custom server URLs on the legacy REST path have no stated TLS enforcement, certificate validation, or URL validation, so credentials and workout data could be sent in cleartext or to an unintended host.
attacks.evidence: "the user has configured a custom server URL"

attacks.claim: Account deletion covers only Cirrus records via the admin API. It does not reach the on-device backup (kept 30+ days), the 90-day tombstones, or legacy self-hosted data, and deletion success is not verified. This is a gap against erasure obligations.
attacks.evidence: "Account deletion removes the Cirrus user record and all synced records via the Cirrus admin API within 30 days."

attacks.claim: The only halt criterion is crash-free sessions. There is no sync-specific health signal (duplicate rate, sync failure, migration failure) and no kill switch or server-side rollback. Data corruption can occur without crashes and already-replicated data cannot be rolled back by the app.
attacks.evidence: "halting if crash-free sessions drop below 99.3%"

attacks.claim: Free-tier fit is asserted at 90k against a 100k cap with about 10% headroom and no growth projection, and no quota or cost contingency. Per-record sync also multiplies request counts, and the single hosted backend has no load monitoring or thundering-herd plan.
attacks.evidence: "free up to 100k monthly active devices; our 90k fits the free tier."

attacks.claim: Tombstone and backup growth are unbounded in the interim with no compaction plan, and the sizing of GPS-track volume and first-sync payloads for 90k devices is absent.
attacks.evidence: "Deletes are tombstones retained 90 days" / "Migration is chunked (500 workouts per batch)"

attacks.claim: The success metrics (80% reduction, 99.5% sync success) have no measured baseline. The 23% figure has no source query, and client-reported success is unreliable exactly when connectivity is poor.
attacks.evidence: "23% of sync-related GitHub issues in the last 6 months" / "Sync success rate (client-reported) >= 99.5%"

attacks.claim: The plan bundles sync engine replacement, vendor SDK adoption, data-model migration, backend deprecation, and legacy protocol sunset into one 5-week build for three contributors, with no decomposition. Two parallel sync paths are maintained until 5.0.
attacks.evidence: "Adopt Cirrus Sync, a mobile offline-first sync SDK" alongside "Legacy REST sync is removed in app 5.0"

attacks.claim: Per-record resumable uploads without a server-side idempotency key do not prevent a retried record from being inserted twice if the first attempt committed server-side, so the duplicate-workout bug may persist.
attacks.evidence: "uploads are resumable at the record level, so a dropped connection never leaves a partial workout."

attacks.claim: Self-hosted users stay on the legacy REST protocol, which the plan says breaks on poor connectivity, and are then forced onto Cirrus Cloud in 5.0 with no migration path, UX, or notice.
attacks.evidence: "app 4.x continues to speak the legacy REST sync protocol when the user has configured a custom server URL."

attacks.claim: The append-only invariant after 'finish' conflicts with per-field LWW edits to title, notes, and gear, and 'finish' is undefined, so the 14 conflict scenarios cannot be verified from the artifact.
attacks.evidence: "Workouts are append-only after the \"finish\" event; edits after finish (title, notes, gear) are per-field last-writer-wins"

attacks.claim: Removing self-hosting is a material change to a public commitment made to ~3,000 self-hosted instances, and the plan gives no notice, deprecation window beyond a loosely dated 5.0, or migration guidance.
attacks.evidence: "planned for end of next year"
